whenToUse: México only. Between friends it's just "dude", said ten times a day, and it can be affectionate or annoyed depending on tone. With a boss, an elder or a stranger it sounds rude. Outside Mexico people may not know it.
México. "¿Neta?" means "really?" and "la neta" is the plain truth. Safe with friends and colleagues, not formal. Nobody will understand it in Spain.
example: La neta, no tengo ganas de salir.

whenToUse: México. Your all-purpose "cool" for things and people. Friendly and safe. Spain says "guay", Colombia "chévere", Chile "bacán"; use the local one when you can.

english: wow! / okay, let's go / come on (Mexico)
whenToUse: México. A multitool: surprise, agreement, encouragement. Safe everywhere in Mexico, informal. Intonation does all the work.
México. Fine with anyone. Don't mix it up with "padre" meaning father, and avoid "¡Qué madre!" which can mean the opposite depending on tone (see the swearing section).

english: right now, in a bit (Latin America)
whenToUse: Latin America, esp. Mexico. It can mean "this very second" or "whenever I get round to it". Ask "¿ahorita ahorita?" if it matters. Safe in any register.
España. Between friends "tío" is "mate" or "dude", used all the time. In Latin America it only means uncle or aunt, so "hola, tío" to a friend will sound odd. Fine with friends, avoid with elders.
España. Completely safe, works with anyone. Latin Americans understand it but would say chido, chévere or bacán instead.
España, casual. "Me mola" is "I dig it". Not used in Latin America. Fine among friends, a bit youthful with elders.
España. The standard "okay", said constantly and very polite. In Latin America say "ok", "dale" or "sale" (Mexico) instead.
España, informal. "Estoy flipando" is "I'm amazed", positive or negative. Fine among friends and colleagues.
example: Flipo con lo caro que está todo.

whenToUse: Colombia, Venezuela, Caribbean, Peru and more. Friendly and safe. Mexico and Spain would say chido and guay.
Chile and Peru. Safe and positive. In Argentina people say "copado" or "bárbaro" instead.
Río de la Plata. Used as a call-out ("che, mirá") or as filler. Friendly everywhere there; it can sound silly when imitated elsewhere.
Río de la Plata. Between close friends it's affectionate, like "dude". To strangers it's a real insult ("idiot"). Mexicans would hear a strong insult; stay away until a local uses it first.
Argentina and Uruguay. Neutral and friendly: "un pibe" is "a guy". Parce (Colombia) and cuate (Mexico) do the same job.
Colombia, especially Medellín. Friendly and informal. Safe with peers, not for formal chats.
Río de la Plata slang for work. Fine in casual talk. Mexicans say "la chamba", Spaniards "el curro".
México, also Peru and Chile. Casual and perfectly acceptable; many people say it all day.
España. Casual, standard among everyone. Not used in Latin America.
example: Salgo del curro a las seis.

whenToUse: México. Casual for money. In Colombia and Chile "plata" is more common; in Argentina "guita".
Texting only. "q" is "que", "xq" or "pq" is "porque / por qué". Perfectly fine for WhatsApp, never in an email to your boss.

english: te quiero mucho, love you lots (texting)
whenToUse: Texting. Safe for friends, family and partners. Avoid with someone you barely know, it can read as romantic.
Texting sign-off. In Spain "un beso" is common even with colleagues; in Latin America "bss" is more for friends and family.
Texting. Very casual and friendly. Skip it in formal messages.
Laughter in writing. Spanish uses j for the h sound, so "hahaha" would look like silent letters. "Jeje" is a mischievous giggle.

España. Everyday in friend groups for anger or surprise, but it's still a swear word. With family, bosses or strangers, don't. In Mexico it's understood but not natural; there people say "chingar" instead.

España and the Caribbean (Cuba, Venezuela, Dominican Republic). Literally a rude word for female anatomy, used as "damn!" Strong. Common in casual speech there, but don't use it with strangers or elders.

México, España. Literally "billy goat". Between close friends it can be a compliment ("qué cabrón eres" = "you're a legend"); in an argument it's a serious insult. Context and tone decide, so avoid it as a learner.

english: idiot, jerk (Mexico, much of Latin America)
whenToUse: México, Central America, Caribbean. Calls someone a fool or a coward. Strong insult with strangers, jokey with friends. In Argentina "pendejo" just means a kid, so check where you are.
México. The most flexible and vulgar word family. "Está chingón" means "it's awesome", "vete a la chingada" is strongly rude. Never in polite company; outside Mexico it sounds odd or aggressive.

english: to take, grab (Spain) / to have sex (much of Latin America)
whenToUse: Danger word. In Spain it's an ordinary verb ("coger el autobús"). In Mexico, Argentina and many other countries it's the vulgar verb for sex. Use "tomar" or "agarrar" in Latin America to be safe.
example: En España: ¿Cogemos el autobús? En México: ¿Tomamos el autobús?

english: wow, how cool; or how awful (Mexico)
whenToUse: México. Tone decides: "está de poca madre" is "awesome", "¡qué poca madre!" is "how rude". Vulgar but extremely common among friends. Avoid with elders or in work settings.
España. Mild, friendly exclamation of surprise or worry. Safe with everyone, even your grandmother.
México. The polite version of a stronger swear. Totally fine with friends and most colleagues. Short "no mames" is the vulgar sibling.
